lessons.title: Housing, handling and biosecurity for pigs
lessons.html:
Pig production basics

Pigs grow fast and breed well, so a well-run piggery can earn good money. But pigs are sensitive to heat, cold, dirt and disease. Good daily husbandry makes the difference between profit and loss. Common breeds in South Africa are the Large White, Landrace and Duroc, and crosses of these.

Housing

  • Temperature - pigs cannot sweat well. Protect them from heat with shade, ventilation, and in hot areas sprinklers or wallows. Piglets need warmth, so farrowing pens have a heat lamp or heated creep area.
  • Space - do not overcrowd. Crowding causes fighting, tail biting and disease.
  • Floors - dry, non-slip and easy to clean. Wet, slippery floors cause leg injuries.
  • Water - clean water at all times from nipple drinkers or troughs. Check drinkers every day; a blocked nipple can cause salt poisoning and death.

Handling pigs

  • Move pigs slowly using a pig board and your voice. Never kick or beat pigs; the Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 makes cruelty an offence.
  • Pigs follow each other, so move them in small groups.
  • Be careful with sows that have piglets and with boars. Both can bite and cause serious injury. Always keep a board between you and the animal and know your escape route.

Biosecurity

African swine fever and other serious diseases can wipe out a whole piggery. African swine fever is a controlled disease under the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984 and must be reported to the state vet.

  • Fence the unit and keep visitors out unless necessary.
  • Shower in or change into clean overalls and boots before entering.
  • Use foot baths with fresh disinfectant.
  • Never feed kitchen or restaurant waste (swill) to pigs. It can carry disease.
  • Keep wild pigs, dogs, rats and birds away from the pigs and feed.

lessons.title: Breeding, farrowing and piglet care
lessons.html:
The breeding sow

A gilt is a young female that has not yet farrowed; a sow has had at least one litter. Pigs come on heat about every 21 days. Signs of heat include a red, swollen vulva, restlessness and the sow standing still when you press firmly on her back (the standing reflex), especially when a boar is nearby.

Pregnancy in pigs lasts about three months, three weeks and three days (about 114 to 115 days). Record the service date so you know when to move the sow to the farrowing house.

Preparing for farrowing

  1. Wash and disinfect the farrowing pen and let it dry.
  2. Wash the sow before she moves in, as the farm programme requires.
  3. Move her into the farrowing crate about a week before the due date so she settles.
  4. Check the heat lamp or creep heating is working.

At farrowing

  • Signs that farrowing is close include nest-building behaviour, restlessness and milk at the teats.
  • Watch quietly. Wipe mucus from piglets' noses if needed and put them to the udder.
  • Call the supervisor if the sow strains for a long time without producing a piglet, as the farm's procedures specify.

Piglet care

  • Make sure every piglet drinks colostrum in the first hours of life.
  • Keep piglets warm in the creep area. Cold piglets lie close to the sow and get crushed.
  • Piglets are born with low iron and need an iron supplement in the first days of life, as the vet or product label directs.
  • Other procedures such as teeth clipping, tail docking or castration must only be done by trained people according to the farm's welfare policy and veterinary advice.
  • Offer creep feed early so piglets get used to solid feed before weaning.

lessons.title: Feeding, growing pigs and daily health checks
lessons.html:
Feeding pigs

Pigs are monogastrics with a simple stomach, so they need balanced feeds high in energy and good protein. Feed is the largest cost in a piggery, so wasting feed means wasting money.

GroupTypical feed
Suckling pigletsSow milk plus creep feed
WeanersWeaner or starter meal
Growers and finishersGrower and finisher meal
Dry sowsLimited sow ration to avoid getting too fat
Lactating sowsLactation ration, fed generously
  • Use the right feed for each group as the feeding programme says.
  • Set feeders so feed does not spill on the floor.
  • Keep feed dry and free of mould. Mouldy feed can contain toxins that cause abortion and poor growth.
  • Change feeds gradually over a few days.

Daily health checks

Walk through every pen at least once a day and look at every pig. Healthy pigs are curious, eat eagerly, have curly tails and firm dung. Report pigs that:

  • Do not come to the feeder or lie apart from the group.
  • Have diarrhoea, cough or breathe heavily.
  • Are lame or have swollen joints.
  • Show red or purple skin patches, especially with high fever.
  • Have bitten tails or wounds.

Move sick pigs to a hospital pen. Treat only as the vet directs and record all treatments. Follow the withdrawal period on the label before any pig goes to the abattoir. Dispose of dead pigs as the farm procedure requires and never sell or eat pigs that died of disease.

Key points

  • Pigs need protection from heat, clean water and dry floors.
  • Strict biosecurity and no swill feeding protect against African swine fever.
  • Pregnancy lasts about 114 days; prepare the farrowing pen in advance.
  • Piglets need colostrum, warmth and an iron supplement.
  • Check every pig daily and report sick animals early.
